films.title: Trapped Alone in Space
films.logline: A scientist, a dying ship, no way home. When contact with Earth goes silent, he has to decide what is worth surviving for.

films.logline: A boy in a small Indian backyard chalks the number 7 onto a rag ball and plays a World Cup final that only exists in his head.

films.title: The Rakhi That Never Breaks

films.logline: He could not understand the language at school. His teachers called him slow. They were wrong.

films.logline: Ramesh has delivered the same red tiffin to the same desk every day for years. Then one day it comes back untouched.

films.title: Ramayana

films.title: Foam Festival — Yamuna, 2026
films.logline: Every year during Chhath Puja, thousands wade into the Yamuna at sunrise. Every year, the river is covered in a thick white foam that looks like fresh snow.
synopsis: Every year during Chhath Puja, thousands of devotees wade into the Yamuna in Delhi to offer arghya at sunrise. Every year, the river is covered in a thick white foam that looks like fresh snow.
The photographs are real, and they are taken every November. The film photographs that morning with total reverence, and then tells you what the white is made of.

The froth forms when untreated sewage and detergent runoff load the river with phosphates and surfactants, which whip into foam wherever the water is churned, usually at barrages and weirs. High ammonia is part of the same picture.
In November 2025 the Delhi Pollution Control Committee recorded zero dissolved oxygen at multiple points on the Delhi stretch of the Yamuna. Zero dissolved oxygen means nothing can live there.
The 22 kilometres between Wazirabad and Okhla make up less than two percent of the river's length and carry roughly eighty percent of its pollution load. That stretch is where people stand.
The people in the water did not put any of this in the river.

films.title: Inside Antilia: What Actually Holds It Up
films.logline: A private tower in the middle of Mumbai. Not the facade everyone photographs, but the structure underneath it.

films.title: Why India's New Parliament Is a Triangle
films.logline: The building is a triangle, and that was a decision. This is the reasoning behind the shape.
synopsis: Every frame in this film is modelled, lit and rendered in 3D.

films.title: Why the Qutub Minar Hasn't Fallen
films.logline: Earthquakes, lightning, centuries of weather. It is still standing, and there are reasons for that.

films.title: Ram Mandir: 56 Layers of Man-Made Rock
films.logline: In December 2020 the test piles under the site failed. Driven 125 feet into the ground, loaded to 700 tonnes, and they still gave way.
synopsis: In December 2020, the test piles under the Ram Mandir site failed. Driven 125 feet into the ground, loaded to 700 tonnes, and they still gave way.

The problem was the site itself. Below roughly 17 metres there was no original soil left, just loose river material sitting on the old course of the Sarayu. You cannot found a stone temple meant to stand for a thousand years on that.

So the engineers did something unusual. They excavated the entire site and rebuilt the ground from scratch: 56 compacted layers of engineered fill fused into a single artificial rock, topped with a granite raft.

Above it sits a temple with no steel anywhere in its structure, because steel corrodes and the design life is measured in centuries, not decades. 392 pillars, interlocking stone joints, pink sandstone.
The film breaks down the engineering, one constraint at a time.
